# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
# Critical Reading: Achterberg et al., Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

**Bottom line:** This is a careful review and the most useful of the four documents. It has a registered protocol, double-coded moderators, separates per-hour from per-worker results, and is honest about how its moderators overlap. Its central estimate of an 8–10% per-hour gain, with output per worker held steady in discretionary work and falling about 9% in coverage-bound work, is well supported. Two claims go beyond the evidence. Its dismissal of novelty rests on four studies compared with each other rather than followed over time. And its explanation of funnel asymmetry as publication bias ignores a more obvious cause: small studies also tend to have weaker designs.

## 1. The numbers check out

- **Counts add up.** 9 controlled + 14 uncontrolled = 23; 8 actual-hours + 15 scheduled = 23; 13 + 7 + 3 work types = 23; 12 record-based + 11 manager-reported = 23.
- **The prediction interval is consistent.** Its centre on the log scale matches the pooled +13.4%. The implied between-study SD (τ ≈ 0.076) fits an I² of 81%.
- **Per-hour and per-worker results roughly agree.** Dividing per-worker by per-hour gives implied hours cuts of about 11% where actual hours were measured, and about 15% where scheduled hours were used. Both are plausible: Varden's actual cuts were 13–17%, and Halden's was about 14%.
- **The overlap figures imply this split:**

| | Uncontrolled (14) | Controlled (9) |
|---|---|---|
| Actual hours | 2 | 6 |
| Scheduled hours | 12 | 3 |
| Record-based output | 5 | 7 |
| Manager-reported | 9 | 2 |

So the "controlled", "actual-hours" and "record-based" subgroups are largely **the same studies**.

## 2. "Convergence" on 8–10% is less independent than it looks

The Discussion says controlled studies (8.2%), actual-hours studies (7.9%), record-based studies (9.7%) and the bias-adjusted estimate (9.1%) "converge". But these groups share most of their members, so their agreement is largely one result counted several times.

The more useful figure is missing: the pooled estimate for studies that are controlled **and** measure actual hours **and** use records. Each of these features is associated with a smaller effect, so that subset could well come in below 8%. With about 5–6 studies it would be imprecise, but it should be reported.

## 3. The duration claim is the main overreach

The abstract says "Effects show no sign of decay over time" and the text says "novelty explanations can therefore be set aside". This rests on four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, pooled at +14.0% (CI 6.2 to 22.4). There are four problems:

- **It compares studies, not time points.** Novelty is about whether an effect fades *within* a study. Comparing long studies with short ones mixes duration with every other difference between them. The right analysis uses within-study trajectories, for example the Varden 24-month follow-up.
- **The estimate is too imprecise.** A CI of 6–22% can't rule out meaningful decay from a true early effect of around 10%.
- **The design mix is unknown.** If the long studies are mostly uncontrolled or use scheduled hours, 14.0% should be compared with the uncontrolled 18.7%, not the overall 13.4%. That comparison would suggest some decline.
- **Survivorship.** Long follow-ups exist only for schemes that continued. Organisations that reverted, like Halden's retail and healthcare cases, drop out.

This mirrors Varga & Holm's error in the opposite direction. They asserted novelty without showing it; this review dismisses it without being able to test it. The honest conclusion is that durability remains **unresolved**.

## 4. Small-study effects: publication bias is not the only explanation

The review reads the funnel asymmetry (Egger p = 0.02) and the trim-and-fill adjustment as publication bias. The alternative is right there in its own data. Small studies are likely to be uncontrolled pilots that use scheduled hours and manager ratings, all of which the review shows are associated with larger effects. Asymmetry produced by real differences between studies looks the same as asymmetry produced by suppressed studies.

Trim-and-fill is also known to perform poorly when heterogeneity is high (I² = 81%), and Egger's test has limited power with k = 23. The review should:

- run Egger's test with design and hours measure included as covariates, and
- present +9.1% as a sensitivity check, not as evidence of suppression.

The adjusted figure happens to land close to the controlled-study estimates. That points to design as the explanation, not unpublished studies.

## 5. The abstract understates the per-worker finding

The abstract reports per-worker change across all studies as −1.8% (CI −4.9 to +1.4), which reads as "no change". In **controlled studies**, the most credible subgroup, output per worker fell by **4.1% (CI −7.6 to −0.5)**, a range that excludes zero. Restricting to controlled discretionary studies gives −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2), so the drop is driven mainly by coverage-bound and mixed settings. That fits the work-type story, but it deserves a place in the abstract.

Per-worker output arguably should have been the **primary** outcome. It doesn't depend on the hours denominator, which is the main source of bias the review identifies. Fifteen of the 23 per-hour estimates divide by scheduled hours, the very method the Halden critique and the Varden authors showed overstates gains.

## 6. Coding and unit-of-analysis questions

- **Varden and Halden.** Varden contains both a discretionary and a coverage-bound stratum, but the work-type counts sum to 23, so each study is coded once. If Varden was coded "mixed", its cleanest contrast is lost to the moderator analysis. If it was assigned one type, half its data is mislabelled. Splitting multi-stratum studies into separate settings would be better. The same question applies to Halden's six sectors.
- **Which Halden figures?** The review says actual hours were used where available. It should state whether it used Halden's published 23.4% or the corrected microdata figures (around 11% in the corrected subset), and how it handled the misreported attrition.
- **Coverage-bound "per-hour gains" again.** "Real but too small to compensate" treats +6.2% as productivity. As discussed for Varden, in work driven by arriving demand this mostly reflects less idle time, paid for by longer queues. The per-worker and service-level figures are the meaningful ones here.
- **Size of the hours cut.** Reductions range from 10% upward, but cut size isn't examined as a moderator. Gains plausibly depend on it.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Fatigue.** The study-level r = 0.18 across 11 studies has a 95% CI of roughly −0.47 to +0.70. It is too imprecise to show fatigue doesn't matter, and it is also an ecological correlation. It does weaken Halden's claim that reduced fatigue is "the most plausible single explanation", but no more than that.
- **Sick leave.** "Fell in all 14 studies" counts direction only. Part of the −31% may be mechanical, since fewer working days means fewer days on which anyone can be off sick.
- **Search size.** 412 records screened is modest. The authors did contact pilot organisers, which helps with grey literature.
- **The response to Varga & Holm is fair.** The controlled and actual-hours subgroups do avoid the selection and measurement problems that re-analysis raised, and their CIs exclude zero. But the review can't rule out the novelty part of that critique, for the reasons in Section 3.

## 8. Fair summary

> Across 23 studies, reduced hours at full pay raise output per hour by roughly 8–10% in the more rigorous studies. Those studies overlap heavily, and an estimate restricted to studies with all three rigorous features is not reported. Headline figures above 20% come from uncontrolled studies that divide by scheduled hours. In controlled studies, output per worker fell by about 4%. In discretionary work the fall was small and not statistically clear (about −3%); in coverage-bound work it was about 9%, so maintaining service requires extra staff. Whether gains last beyond a year cannot be determined from four between-study comparisons. The mechanism, whether rest, cutting low-value work such as meetings, or something else, is untested.

## Across all four documents

| Question | Halden pilot | Varden trial | Varga & Holm | Meta-analysis | Best current answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain | +23.4% | +12.5% / +6.7% | ~11%, "entirely artifact" | +8–10% | **Roughly 8–12% in discretionary work, measured against actual hours** |
| Per-worker output | ~−1% | −2% / −11% | — | −4% (controlled) | **Roughly flat to slightly down (discretionary); about −9 to −11% (coverage)** |
| Sector-general? | Yes | No | No | No | **No: it depends on whether output is tied to presence** |
| Durable? | Assumed | Follow-up pending | No (asserted) | Yes (asserted) | **Unknown: Varden's 24-month results are the key test** |
| Mechanism | Fatigue | Meetings (exploratory) | Novelty | Untested | **Unknown: meetings is the leading testable hypothesis** |

Each successive document corrected real errors in the earlier ones, and each overstated something of its own: sector-generality, artifact, or no decay. The pattern that holds across all of them is the distinction between discretionary and coverage-bound work, together with the gap between scheduled and actual hours.
